Jacobian-Free Krylov-Arnoldi Framework for Static
V oltage Stability Estimation of Power Systems
With 100% Renewable Energy
Guoteng Wang
 , Member, IEEE, Ying Huang
 , Senior Member, IEEE, Chongyu Wang
 , Member, IEEE,
and Mohammad Shahidehpour
 , Life Fellow, IEEE
Abstract—The pervasive adoption of inverter-interfaced
resources in 100% renewable power systems fundamentally
alters voltage regulation dynamics and renders classical margin-
estimation techniques computationally prohibitive. This paper
introduces a uniﬁed, Jacobian-free Krylov-Arnoldi (JFKA)
framework for automated estimation of system static voltage sta-
bility (SVS). First, inverter current-limiting behavior is captured
by a smooth S-type function, preserving continuous power-ﬂow
structure across both grid-forming (GFM) and grid-following
(GFL) control modes. Building on singularity theory, we derive
a Jacobian-free stability indicator that pinpoints the onset of
voltage collapse without explicit derivative evaluation. To e ﬃ-
ciently solve the resulting large-scale, transcendental power-ﬂow
equations, we embed a reduced-order Arnoldi process within a
Newton-Krylov solver, yielding rapid convergence and markedly
lower memory footprint. Case studies on a modiﬁed IEEE-39 bus
network with full renewable penetration demonstrate that our
method accurately tracks voltage regulation limits under varied
load-growth scenarios and automatic mode switches.
Note to Practitioners —As grids reach 100% renewable energy
penetration, real-time voltage regulation capability estimation
must handle inverter mode switching and large-scale nonlinear
solves. This work introduces a JFKA solver that uses an S-type
function for smooth current-limit modeling and a singularity-
based indicator for collapse detection. Integrated into existing
EMS/DA tools, it enables continuous margin tracking under
load growth and mode shifts. The framework runs on standard
desktop hardware and scales to large power grids, o ﬀering plug-
and-play deployment for automated voltage regulation capability
assessment.
Index Terms —Power systems with 100% renewable energy,
voltage regulation capability estimation, renewable energy
sources, Jacobian-free Krylov-Arnoldi framework.
I. I NTRODUCTION
T
HE urgent need to mitigate climate change has placed
the decarbonization of electrical power systems at the
forefront of global energy policy. As nations commit to

increasingly ambitious zero-carbon targets, the transition to
power systems comprised entirely of renewable energy sources
(REPSs) is accelerating worldwide [1], [2]. In these 100%
REPSs, conventional synchronous generators (SGs) are being
displaced by inverter-interfaced wind and solar installations,
resulting in fundamental shifts in both operational paradigms
and system dynamics [3]. Numerous regions—including major
economies—have pledged to achieve full renewable supply by
2050, underscoring the urgency and scale of this transforma-
tion [4], [5], [6].
Unlike SGs, inverter-based resources regulate power ﬂow
by modulating DC voltages through power electronic switch-
ing. This introduces stringent current limits, necessary for
protecting sensitive semiconductor devices from thermal
and electrical stress [9]. As grid conditions evolve—such
as ﬂuctuating bus voltages and rising demand—inverters
must dynamically switch between grid-forming (GFM) and
grid-following (GFL) modes. During periods of stress, current-
limiting action further constrains their ability to provide
reactive power support. These nonlinear and mode-dependent
behaviors present new technical challenges for system opera-
tors, particularly in the context of static voltage stability (SVS)
estimation across large-scale, highly renewable grids.
Historically, SVS estimation has relied on classical method-
ologies such as continuation power ﬂow (CPF) and voltage-
sensitivity analysis, which utilize explicit Jacobian matrix
calculations and track system stability margins via model-
based rollbacks at detected bifurcation points [10], [11]. While
advanced methods—including holomorphic embedding [12]
and load-impedance modulus margin techniques [13]—have
improved computational e ﬃciency in SG-dominated environ-
ments, they are inherently limited. These approaches often
assume idealized voltage sources, and lack the ﬂexibility to
accommodate the continuous, nonlinear control-mode transi-
tions and current-limiting e ﬀects intrinsic to inverter-based
grids. As a result, they are increasingly ill-suited for real-time
monitoring and margin estimation in future REPSs.
Recent research e ﬀorts have begun to address the uncer-
tainty inherent in renewable generation, employing Monte
Carlo simulations [14], global sensitivity analysis [15], matrix
factorization [16], and advanced weather-informed risk assess-
ments [17]. However, these studies predominantly focus on
stochastic variability in generation, rather than the structural
and dynamical changes in voltage regulation mechanisms

introduced by inverter control. The evolving landscape of
inverter controls—spanning GFM and GFL paradigms, with
subcategories such as PQ and PV modes [18], [19]—has a
profound impact on system voltage support, particularly under
operational stress or rapid switching. While some recent works
extend Jacobian formulations [21] or incorporate voltage sta-
bility constraints in unit commitment [22], many continue to
treat inverter control modes as static, neglecting the dynamic
transitions induced by real-time current limiting [23]. This
oversimpliﬁcation can introduce signiﬁcant errors, especially
when estimating SVS near operational boundaries.
Current strategies to model control-mode switching often
rely on discrete rollback mechanisms: transition points are
detected, the power-ﬂow model is updated, and analysis
resumes [24]. While feasible for small networks, this approach
becomes computationally intractable in large-scale systems
due to the combinatorial growth of model variants and the
potential for algorithmic instability. More speciﬁcally, CPF
methods [10], [11] su ﬀer from high computational cost due
to repeated Jacobian evaluations and step size control, making
them less suitable for large-scale or real-time applications.
Holomorphic embedding techniques [12] may encounter con-
vergence and truncation errors in highly nonlinear systems
with extensive inverter penetration. Approaches relying on
static inverter models [23] cannot capture the dynamic mode-
switching and current-limiting e ﬀects of modern inverters,
leading to inaccurate SVS estimation under stress or rapid
operating changes. Consequently, two major challenges remain
unresolved: (1) integrating a continuous representation of
mode-switching behavior into SVS estimation without resort-
ing to discrete model updates, and (2) developing a scalable,
Jacobian-free computational solver capable of real-time appli-
cation in large, complex power networks.
Against this backdrop, this paper presents a uniﬁed
Jacobian-Free Krylov-Arnoldi (JFKA) framework for auto-
mated voltage regulation capability estimation in 100%
renewable power systems. Our approach is distinguished by
the following key innovations:
1) Jacobian-free collapse indicator: By leveraging sin-
gularity theory, we develop a robust stability indicator
that detects proximity to voltage collapse using trends in
the minimum singular value of Jacobian-vector products.
This obviates the need for explicit derivative calcula-
tions, dramatically reducing computational overhead.
2) Newton-Krylov solver with reduced-order Arnoldi
process: We embed a low-dimensional Arnoldi process
within each Newton iteration, enabling e ﬃcient and
memory-frugal solution of the large-scale and transcen-
dental power-ﬂow equations characteristic of REPSs.
3) Continuous mode-switching modeling: The pro-
posed framework captures the e ﬀect of control mode
transitions—induced by inverter current limiting—on
SVS estimation, ensuring accuracy and robustness even
under rapid and large-scale operational changes.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
Section II explores the impact of inverter control mode switch-
ing on SVS. Section III introduces the proposed JFKA method.
Section IV presents comprehensive case studies on a modiﬁed
Fig. 1. Single-RES system.
IEEE-39 bus system with full renewable penetration. Finally,
Section V concludes with a summary of key ﬁndings and
future research directions.

Assuming that the power factor of the load keeps
unchanged, then the voltage magnitude of the load bus is
proportional to the active load. In the PV plane, the power-
voltage characteristic of the RES is represented by a straight
line crossing the origin. The PV curve considering the RES
current limitation is shown in Fig. 2, and the system parame-
ters are presented in Table I.
As the load increases from 0, the voltage magnitude of the
load bus will decrease from the initial value Es. When the
voltage of the load bus decreases to a small value, the required
current will exceed the limit of the RES, which will cause
the RES to change from constant voltage control mode to
constant current control mode. If the capacity of RES is not
large enough, (set to 2.0 pu in this case), then the RES will
switch before the operating point reaches the saddle point. In
Fig. 2, when the operating point reaches the mode switching
point, as the load impedance decreases, the operating point
will shift from the PV curve in constant voltage control mode
to the PV curve in constant current control mode. If the load
impedance continues to decrease, the system operating point
will move toward the origin along the PV curve in constant
current control mode. In this case, the load limit of the system
is not at the saddle point, but at the mode switching point. If
the capacity of the RES is large enough (set to 5.0 pu in this
case), then the PV curve in constant current control mode will
be below the saddle point. As the load impedance decreases,
the operating point of the system will ﬁrst reach the saddle
point, and then reach the control mode switching point after
crossing the saddle point. In this case, the load limit of the
system is still at the saddle point.

B. Jacobian-Free Voltage Stability Criterion
The singularity of the Jacobian matrix is often utilized as
a criterion for judging the voltage stability of the system. If
the Jacobian matrix is singular, it indicates that the power
ﬂow equation has no solution, which physically manifests
as voltage collapse. The research on continuous power ﬂow
has proved that the singular point of the Jacobian matrix is
consistent with the saddle point of the PV curve. In traditional
power systems dominated by SGs, the form of the power
ﬂow equation is relatively simple, making it easy to derive
the Jacobian matrix. In 100% REPSs, the S-type function
brings great di ﬃculties to generating the Jacobian matrix. To
solve this problem, a Jacobian-free voltage stability criterion
is proposed below.

While a straightforward approach to assessing voltage sta-
bility is to attempt solving the power ﬂow equations at
incrementally increased load levels, this method faces substan-
tial challenges in inverter-dominated systems. The presence of
continuous mode switching and strong nonlinearities can cause
commercial solvers to either fail to converge prematurely or
miss the true stability boundary. Moreover, such a brute-force
approach is computationally intensive for large systems. The
proposed Jacobian-free algorithm not only improves compu-
tational eﬃciency and robustness, but also enables continuous
and accurate stability margin tracking, which is critical for
real-time system monitoring and control in 100% renewable
power grids.

B. Veriﬁcation of The Jacobian-Free Voltage Stability
Criterion
Generally speaking, the voltage instability is equivalent to
the insolvability of the power ﬂow equations, another manifes-
tation is the singularity of the Jacobian matrix. In this paper,
a Jacobian-free voltage stability criterion is proposed. The
proposed criterion avoids the establishment of the Jacobian
matrix, and estimates the voltage stability by judging the
singularity of matrix (15), which can be obtained by (16). To
verify the e ﬀectiveness of the Jacobian-free voltage stability
criterion, the relationship between the singularity of matrix
(15) and the voltage stability is studied below.
The variation of the minimum singular value of matrix (15)
with the load increasing coe ﬃcient in two cases are shown
in Fig. 6. In Case 1, only the active load increases with the
load increasing coe ﬃcient, while the reactive load remains
unchanged. In Case 2, both the active load and reactive
load increase with the load increasing coe ﬃcient. It can be
seen from Fig. 6 that with the load increasing, the minimum
singular value of matrix (15) decreases continuously. Then we
can conclude that the Jacobian-free voltage stability criterion
can accurately evaluate the voltage stability of the system. As
per Fig. 6, when the power ﬂow equation has no solution,
the minimum singular value of matrix (15) is at a very small
value. Therefore, the e ﬀectiveness of the proposed Jacobian-
free voltage stability criterion is veriﬁed.

V. C ONCLUSION
This paper presents a uniﬁed JFKA framework for SVS
estimation in 100% REPSs, explicitly considering the con-
trol mode switching behavior of RESs. By introducing a
smooth S-type function to model inverter current limiting and
developing a singularity-based, Jacobian-free voltage stabil-
ity criterion, the proposed method e ﬀectively addresses the
nonlinear and mode-dependent challenges inherent to 100%
RESPs. The integration of a reduced-order Arnoldi process
within a Newton-Krylov solver enables e ﬃcient and memory-
saving solutions for large-scale, transcendental power ﬂow
equations. Comprehensive case studies on a modiﬁed IEEE-39
bus system demonstrate that the JFKA framework accurately
tracks SVS under various load growth scenarios and control
mode transitions. Results conﬁrm that inverter current limiting
